{{short description|Dutch-American mathematician}}
[[File:ArnoldDresden.jpg|thumb|right|Prof. Arnold Dresden at Swarthmore College]]
'''Arnold Dresden''' (1882–1954) was a Dutch-American mathematician, known for his work in the [[calculus of variations]] and collegiate mathematics education.<ref>{{cite journal|author=David E. Zitarelli|author-link=David E. Zitarelli|title=In the Shadow of Giants: A Section of American Mathematicians, 1925-1950|journal=Mathematics Magazine|date=June 2005|volume=78|issue=3|pages=175–191|jstor=30044154|doi=10.2307/30044154}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Edith R. Schneckenburger|title=News and Notices|journal=Amer. Math. Monthly|volume=61|issue=7|year=1954|pages=497–498|jstor=2308099}}</ref> He was a president of the [[Mathematical Association of America]] and a member of the [[American Philosophical Society]].<ref>[http://www.maa.org/history/presidents/dresden.html MAA presidents: Arnold Dresden]</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=APS Member History |url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Arnold+Dresden&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced |access-date=2023-06-26 |website=search.amphilsoc.org}}</ref>

==Background==
Dresden was born in [[Amsterdam]] on November 23, 1882, into a wealthy banking family. After matriculating for three years at the [[University of Amsterdam]] he used tuition money in 1903 to book passage on a ship to New York City. He then traveled to Chicago to help a friend, arriving 
there on his 21st birthday. Two years later, after saving money from working at various jobs, he enrolled in the graduate program at the [[University of Chicago]], where he earned his Ph.D. in 1909 under the direction of [[Oskar Bolza]] with thesis ''The Second Derivatives of the Extremal Integral''.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=5887}}</ref>

==Research and teaching==
Dresden taught at the [[University of Wisconsin]] 1909–1927. During this time he wrote several papers on the calculus of variations and systems of linear differential equations. He directed one doctoral dissertation. He was elected a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] in 1911.<ref>{{cite web|title=Historic Fellows|website=Association for the Advancement of Science|url=https://www.aaas.org/fellows/historic}} (Search on last name "Dresden".)</ref> He was recruited to [[Swarthmore College]] by [[Frank Aydelotte|President Frank Aydelotte]] to initiate an honors program in mathematics that ended up being a model for other colleges and universities throughout the U.S. Dresden remained at the elite Quaker college until retiring in 1952; he was adored by many of his students. He was a [[Guggenheim Fellow]] for the academic years 1930–1931 and 1934–1935.<ref>{{cite web|title=Arnold Dresden|website=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation|url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/arnold-dresden/}}</ref> In 1935–1936 he was on sabbatical at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]], where he wrote ''An Invitation to Mathematics''.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://library.ias.edu/files/pdfs/ar/publicationsofme00inst.pdf |title=page 33, Publications of members, 1930–1954 Libraries, Institute for Advanced Study |access-date=2013-01-30 |archive-date=2013-05-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130521155539/http://library.ias.edu/files/pdfs/ar/publicationsofme00inst.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>[http://cdm.itg.ias.edu/cdm/search/searchterm/Arnold Search on "Arnold Dresden" to find directory listing for Arnold Dresden as a Visiting Member of the Institute for Advanced Study.]</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Bennett, Albert A.|journal=Science|volume=84|issue=2189|page=535|title=Review of ''An Invitation to mathematics'' by Arnold Dresden|doi=10.1126/science.84.2189.535.a}}</ref> He died on April 10, 1954, in [[Swarthmore, Pennsylvania]], at age 71.
 
While at Wisconsin Arnold Dresden was active in and served as secretary of, the Chicago Section of the [[American Mathematical Society]]. A charter member of the Mathematical Association of America, he was elected President for 1933–1934. He also served as Vice-President during 1931 and as a member of the Board of Governors for 1935–1940 and 1943–1945. His retiring presidential address, “A program for mathematics",<ref>{{cite journal|author=Dresden, Arnold|title=A Program for Mathematics|journal=Amer. Math. Monthly|date=Apr 1935|volume=42|issue=4|pages=198–208|jstor=2302098|doi=10.2307/2302098}}</ref> encapsulated his deep concern about the place of mathematics in general culture and about the mathematical community's laissez-faire attitude toward the role it should play. A recurring theme was his belief that abstract concepts can be grasped by young people, which he preached in his 1936 book, ''An Invitation to Mathematics''. He was also known as an ally to women in the field, as well.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Murray|first1=Margaret|title=Women Being Mathematicians:Creating a Professional Identity in Post-World War II America|date=2001|publisher=MIT Press|page=244|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Sz78C8-PGUQC&q=kentucky+women+mathematicians&pg=PA262|accessdate=12 February 2018|isbn=9780262632461}}</ref> He also wrote three textbooks and translated [[Bartel Leendert van der Waerden|van der Waerden]]’s classic ''Science Awakening'' from Dutch into English.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Sarton, George|author-link=George Sarton|journal=Isis|volume=46|number=4|pages=368–369|title=Review of ''Science Awakening'' by B. L. Van der Waerden, translated by Arnold Dresden|date=December 1955|doi=10.1086/348434}}</ref>
